name: Ifo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Lynch, John. 1983. Utaha. In Lynch (ed.), Studies in the languages of Erromango (Pacific Linguistics C-79). Archive.org copy (studiesinlanguag0079unse) is access-restricted; fulltext search blocked.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The linguistic history of Southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 1.5.2 p.9: 'Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango' -- a generalisation over the described Erromangan languages (Sye, Ura); ch.2 states Utaha data are excluded from the Proto Erromango phonology discussion as 'the most fragmentary of data'. No Utaha-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Gordon, J. D. 1889. Grammar of the Eromangan dialects, pp. 78-84 (within the Eromangan sketch). In D. Macdonald (ed.), South Sea languages, vol. I: Three New Hebrides languages (Efatese, Eromangan, Santo). Melbourne: Edgerton and Moore / Melbourne Public Library.
sources.note: The only primary data on Utaha: numerals, pronoun/possessive tables, one verb paradigm, c.40 words and the Lord's Prayer in parallel Ura/Utaha columns. No remark on pronunciation, accent or stress anywhere in the Eromangan section (the 'pronounced' remarks in the volume are in the Efatese section).

sources.citation: Lynch, John & Terry Crowley. 2001. Languages of Vanuatu: a new survey and bibliography. Pacific Linguistics 517. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage PL6211.V36 L96 2001
sources.note: Survey entry sec. 3.12.2 pp.124-125: Utaha phonology documentation = 'no'; the only published primary data are Gordon 1889:78-84, interpreted by Lynch 1983; last speaker's two exercise books lost; a few words in Taki's and Crowley's unpublished notes. Also notes 'Ifo' (Grimes 1996) is merely a village name near Ipota. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Lynch, John (ed.). 1983. Studies in the languages of Erromango. PL C-79 -- Introduction (ch.1), sec. 1.3 Location.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; used only for the identity of Utaha vs 'Ifo' (Capell 1962:221 'a southern dialect (Ifo, replacing the older Utaha)'; Gordon MS places Utaha c. five miles north of Dillon's Bay).

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 1983. Utaha. In John Lynch (ed.), Studies in the languages of Erromango, 184-190. Pacific Linguistics C-79. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C79.184 (online ed. 2015, CC BY-SA 4.0, sealang/CRCL).
sources.note: Sec. 1 Phonology, p.185: explicitly says that because of the nature of the data (Gordon 1889's written snippets only) nothing can be said about stress or other suprasegmentals; p.184 'Gordon makes absolutely no statement about Utaha pronunciation at all'. Consonant/vowel inventory reconstructed from orthography only.

sources.citation: Crowley, Terry. n.d. Unpublished Erromango fieldnotes (a handful of words reported to be Utaha), cited in Lynch & Crowley 2001:125; and the lost exercise books of the last Utaha speaker (d. 1954).

sources.note: The only conceivable sources of spoken-form Utaha data; the exercise books are reported lost and the fieldnotes unpublished (Crowley d. 2005; papers possibly at PARADISEC/Waikato).

sources.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1997. What happened to Erromango's languages? Journal of the Polynesian Society 106(1): 33-66.
